doctrine: The Ascension and Heavenly Session of Christ
summary: Christ’s bodily ascension to the Father, his enthronement at God’s right hand, and his present priestly ministry of intercession
readingInstruction: Read Acts 1:1-11 slowly, then turn to Hebrews 4:14-16. Today is a doctrinal pause, so you are reading two passages together: Luke’s account of Jesus rising into the clouds, and the author of Hebrews telling us what that ascension means for the weak and weary. Ask as you read: where did Jesus go, and what is he doing there now?
settingTheScene: For forty days after his resurrection, Jesus appeared to his disciples, proving he was alive and teaching them about the kingdom of God. Yesterday’s reading closed that season of appearances and opened the book of Acts, which is Luke’s second volume. His first volume told what Jesus began to do and teach. Acts tells what he continues to do through his Spirit and his church. But first he must leave. Today we stand on the Mount of Olives with eleven confused men, watching their risen Lord lifted up and taken out of sight. Most Christians celebrate Christmas and Easter. Far fewer know what to do with the ascension. This day exists to correct that, because the ascension is where the story of the resurrection becomes the story of Christ’s reign.
observation: Luke calls his Gospel an account of “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (v. 1), which implies that Acts records what Jesus continues to do.
Jesus gave “many proofs” that he was alive during forty days (v. 3). The resurrection was physical and public.
The disciples ask whether Jesus will now restore the kingdom to Israel (v. 6). They are still thinking in small, national terms.
Jesus does not deny the kingdom. He redirects them to the Spirit’s power and their witness “to the end of the earth” (vv. 7-8).
Jesus is “lifted up” while they are looking, and a cloud takes him from their sight (v. 9).
Two men in white tell them Jesus will return “in the same way” as they saw him go (v. 11).
Hebrews 4:14 says Jesus “has passed through the heavens.” The ascension is described as a journey with a destination.
Hebrews 4:15-16 draws a pastoral conclusion: because Jesus sympathizes with weakness, we may draw near to the throne of grace with confidence.
doctrinalFocus:
The ascension is the event in which the risen Lord Jesus Christ, in his glorified human body, departed from this earth and was received into heaven, where he now sits at the right hand of the Father. It is both a real event on a real day and the beginning of a real, ongoing ministry. The Apostles’ Creed confesses it plainly: “He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of God the Father Almighty.”

Scripture gives us several truths about the ascension. First, it was bodily. The same Jesus who ate fish with his disciples was taken up. He did not shed his humanity like a costume once the mission was finished. A man now reigns at the right hand of God, and he will remain a man forever. This is astonishing good news for human beings, because it means our nature has been carried into the presence of God and honored there.

Second, the ascension is enthronement. In the ancient world, to sit at the right hand of a king was to share his authority. Psalm 110:1 anticipates it: “The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” Peter will preach in Acts 2 that this is exactly what happened to Jesus. Paul says in Ephesians 1:20-22 that God seated Christ above every rule, authority, power, and dominion, and put all things under his feet. The crucified carpenter is Lord of all. This is why the church can speak with confidence in a hostile world: the throne of heaven is not empty or contested. Christ reigns now, even though the full visible evidence of his reign awaits his return.

Third, the ascension inaugurates his priestly intercession. Hebrews insists that Jesus is our great high priest who has passed through the heavens. Under the old covenant, the high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year with blood, and then he left. Christ has entered the true heavenly sanctuary with his own blood, and he does not need to leave again. Romans 8:34 says he is “at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.” Your Savior is not distant or indifferent. He is your advocate before the Father right now.

Fourth, the ascension makes the gift of the Spirit possible. Jesus told his disciples it was to their advantage that he go away, because if he did not, the Helper would not come (John 16:7). Pentecost is the ascended Christ pouring out his Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33). The church’s power in mission is the power of a reigning king.

Fifth, the ascension guarantees a future. The angels said he will come back in the same way. The ascended Christ is also the returning Christ. Between the ascension and the return, the church lives as a people who are sent. We are not left to guard a memory. We are sent to bear witness to a living king.

Some Christians treat the ascension as an awkward epilogue to Easter, as if Jesus got his body back and then needed to be gotten rid of. Scripture treats it as a coronation. The resurrection shows that death is defeated. The ascension shows that the one who defeated it now rules. If the cross is where Christ paid for sin and the resurrection is where he was vindicated, the ascension is where he took his seat, because the work is finished.
interpretation:
Luke opens Acts by looking back and looking forward. Looking back, he reminds Theophilus that his first book dealt with “all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day when he was taken up.” The word “began” is important. If the Gospel was only the beginning, then Acts is not the story of what the apostles did but of what the risen Jesus keeps doing, now from heaven, by his Spirit, through his people.

The disciples’ question in verse 6 reveals how slowly they understood. They had just spent forty days hearing about the kingdom from the risen Lord, and they still asked if he would restore Israel’s national fortunes now. Jesus does not rebuke the hope. He reorders it. The kingdom will come, but the timeline belongs to the Father. In the meantime, they will receive power from the Holy Spirit and be witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the end of the earth. This verse is the outline of the whole book of Acts. The kingdom advances not by political restoration but by the Spirit-empowered testimony of ordinary people.

Then Jesus rises. Luke writes it with restraint. There is no spectacle, no fireworks. He is lifted up, a cloud receives him, and the disciples keep staring at the sky. The cloud is not incidental. Throughout Scripture, a cloud is where God’s glory dwells: the pillar in the wilderness, the cloud that filled the tabernacle, the cloud on the mount of transfiguration. Daniel 7:13 sees “one like a son of man” coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting dominion. The cloud tells the careful reader that Jesus is entering the glory of God, and that Daniel’s vision has begun to come true.

The two men in white interrupt the staring. “Why do you stand looking into heaven?” It is a gentle rebuke, and it is also a promise. This same Jesus will come in the same way. The disciples do not need to scan the sky because they have a job to do and a future to expect.

Hebrews 4:14-16 tells us what Jesus is doing in the meantime. “We have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens.” The author is writing to weary believers who were tempted to drift back to the familiar comforts of the old covenant. His answer is to point them upward. The One who went up is a priest, which means he is on your behalf, now, before God. He is not a priest who stands aloof. Verse 15 says he can sympathize with our weaknesses, “one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.” He knows what it is to be tired, hungry, betrayed, and afraid. His ascended glory has not made him forget what it felt like.

Verse 16 is the invitation. “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace.” Notice the combination of words: throne and grace. A throne suggests authority and judgment. Grace suggests undeserved favor. In the ascension, the two meet. The King who sits on the throne is the one who died for you. When you come before him, you do not find a stern judge reviewing your record but a priest who has already settled it. So you can come with confidence, which does not mean arrogance but boldness, and you will receive mercy for your past and grace for your needs.
connection: Psalm 110 is the Old Testament backbone of this day. David writes, “The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.” The New Testament quotes this verse more than any other Old Testament text, nearly always about the ascension. Daniel 7 provides the cloud and the Son of Man receiving dominion. Leviticus 16 provides the picture of the high priest entering the Most Holy Place with blood, which Hebrews says Christ has fulfilled. Looking forward, Acts 2 will show Peter explaining Pentecost as the work of the ascended Christ, and Revelation 5 will show the Lamb standing at the center of the throne.
application:
First, let the ascension settle where Jesus is. When life feels out of control, remember that someone is on the throne, and he is the one who loves you. Your circumstances do not outrank his authority.

Second, take your failures and weakness to him without delay. Hebrews says come with confidence. If you have been avoiding prayer because you feel unworthy, you have misunderstood the throne. It is a throne of grace. Tell him exactly what you are struggling with. He has been there.

Third, take comfort that Jesus is praying for you right now. Romans 8:34 says so. On days when you feel you cannot pray, the ascended Christ is already interceding.

Fourth, remember that you have been sent. The disciples were told to stop staring at the sky and start witnessing. Ask God this week to give you one specific opportunity to speak of Christ to someone, and then look for it.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for ascending and sitting at the Father’s right hand.
Thank him that he is your king and your high priest.
Ask him to give you confidence to come to his throne of grace.
